references.text: Jesus encourages giving alms from what one has, so that everything may be made clean. Using wealth to help others is a practical way of making 'friends,' cf. Luke 11:41.

Jesus says, 'Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide yourselves with purses that do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in heaven.' This directly connects to the idea of using earthly wealth to secure an eternal home, cf. Luke 12:33.
Inviting the poor and weak to a meal, those who cannot repay, parallels using wealth generously so as to receive reward at the resurrection of the righteous, cf. Luke 14:13–14.
Paul urges the rich to be generous and share with others, so that they lay up treasure as a firm foundation for the future, cf. 1 Timothy 6:17–19.
Jesus contrasts 'unrighteous mammon' with true wealth: If you are not faithful in unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you what is truly valuable? cf. Luke 16:11.
No one can serve both God and mammon. The verse highlights the tension between earthly wealth and service to God, cf. Luke 16:13.
'Whoever shows mercy to the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay them for their good deed.' Using wealth to help others is seen as an investment with God Himself, cf. Proverbs 19:17.
Daniel advises King Nebuchadnezzar to atone for his sins by showing mercy to the poor—righteousness through generosity, cf. Daniel 4:27.
Jesus says that in His Father's house there are many rooms (dwelling places). The expression 'eternal dwellings' in Luke 16:9 points toward the eternal home with God, cf. John 14:2.
Jesus urges not to store up treasures on earth, but in heaven. Using mammon rightly is investing in heavenly treasures, cf. Matthew 6:19–20.

In the parable of the judgment, the righteous are welcomed into the eternal kingdom because they helped the least—giving food, drink, clothing, and visitation. Using one's resources for others leads to being received into eternity, cf. Matthew 25:34–40.
